q: Where does SysTick live, and how does that differ from TIM3?
choices: In the ARM core at 0xE000E010, the same on every Cortex-M
In ST's peripheral space at 0x40000400, right beside TIM3
In the NVIC block at 0xE000E100, wired as an ordinary IRQ 15
In ST's RCC block, so its address differs on each STM32 part
why: SysTick is part of the Cortex-M core, at 0xE000E010 on every Cortex-M. That is why every RTOS uses it as a heartbeat. TIM3 is ST silicon at 0x40000400.

q: Which bit of SysTick CTRL is COUNTFLAG?
why: CTRL holds ENABLE (bit 0), TICKINT (bit 1), CLKSOURCE (bit 2) and COUNTFLAG (bit 16). Bit 24 is not a CTRL field; LOAD and VAL use bits 23:0.

q: What does the TICKINT bit of SysTick CTRL do?
choices: Makes each wrap to 0 raise the SysTick exception
Selects the core clock instead of the external one
Starts the counter counting down from LOAD
Records that the counter has wrapped since the last read
why: TICKINT (bit 1) enables the interrupt. ENABLE (bit 0) starts counting, CLKSOURCE (bit 2) picks the clock, and COUNTFLAG (bit 16) is the wrap flag.

q: Which way does SysTick's VAL count, and what does writing VAL do?
choices: Down to 0; any write clears it
Up to LOAD; any write sets it to LOAD
Down to 0; a write loads the value written
why: VAL counts down and any write clears it to 0, whatever value is written. It does not load the written value; LOAD holds the reload value.

q: How wide are SysTick's LOAD and VAL registers?
why: LOAD and VAL use bits 23:0 only, so the longest period is 2²⁴ clocks. The timers TIM3 and TIM14 are the 16-bit ones.

q: SysTick_Config(SystemCoreClock / 1000) at 48 MHz leaves which value in LOAD?
why: LOAD holds period − 1: 48 000 000 / 1000 = 48 000 clocks, so LOAD = 47 999. 48000 is the classic forgotten −1.

q: A 1 ms SysTick tick on a chip still at its 12 MHz reset clock needs which LOAD?
why: 12 000 000 / 1000 = 12 000 clocks per ms, and LOAD = ticks − 1 = 11 999. 47999 is the 48 MHz value.

q: What is the longest SysTick period at 48 MHz?
why: 2²⁴ clocks / 48 MHz ≈ 0.35 s. 1.4 s would be at 12 MHz, 65.5 ms is a 16-bit microsecond timer's wrap, and 49.7 days is the uint32_t millisecond counter's wrap.

q: What value does SysTick_Config() leave in CTRL?
why: CTRL = CLKSOURCE | TICKINT | ENABLE = bits 2, 1, 0 = 0x7. COUNTFLAG is a status bit the hardware sets, not something SysTick_Config writes.

q: Which NVIC priority does SysTick_Config() give SysTick on this chip?
why: It sets (1 << __NVIC_PRIO_BITS) − 1 = 3 with 2 priority bits: the lowest. Time-keeping is rarely the most urgent thing; a late tick is still counted.

q: What must SysTick_Handler do to acknowledge its interrupt?
choices: Nothing: taking the exception acknowledges it
Write 1 to COUNTFLAG to clear the request
Write 0 to COUNTFLAG, the timer convention
Read VAL, which clears the pending request
why: SysTick_Handler has no flag to clear, unlike every other handler in the course; its request is the wrap itself. Inventing a clear for it is the trap.

q: Lesson 05 polled COUNTFLAG to count milliseconds. Why did that clock lose time?
choices: COUNTFLAG remembers only one wrap, so the extra wraps vanish
COUNTFLAG clears itself after 1 µs, before the loop gets to read it
Polling reads VAL, and every read of VAL restarts the count from LOAD
The poll ran at a lower NVIC priority than the printf did
why: COUNTFLAG records only one wrap. While a printf blocks for ~8 ms, seven more wraps happen and only one is remembered. Reading VAL does not reset it; writing does.

q: A polled 1 ms clock is stuck in a printf of 90 characters at 115 200 baud. About how many milliseconds does it lose?
why: 90 bytes × 86.8 µs ≈ 7.8 ms. COUNTFLAG keeps one of the ~8 wraps, so about 7 ms vanish. The interrupt-driven ms_ticks++ loses none.

q: A uint32_t millisecond counter wraps after about how long?
why: 2³² ms ≈ 4.29 × 10⁹ ms ≈ 49.7 days. 65.5 s is a uint16_t millisecond counter; 24.9 days is where a signed int32 turns negative.

q: Which timeout test is correct even when the millisecond counter wraps?
why: Unsigned subtraction is modulo 2³², so now − start is the true elapsed time even across the wrap. Comparing absolute times, as in the other three, breaks on day 50.

q: start = 0xFFFFFF00 and millis() now returns 0x00000100. What is millis() − start, and has a 500 ms timeout expired?
why: 0x100 − 0xFFFFFF00 = 0x200 = 512 modulo 2³², and 512 ≥ 500. Unsigned arithmetic never goes negative.

q: start = 0xFFFFFE00, now = 0x00000100. Elapsed time by now − start?
why: 0x100 − 0xFFFFFE00 = 0x300 = 768: 0x200 (512) before the wrap plus 0x100 (256) after it.

q: start = 0xFFFFFF00 and the code waits with if (millis() >= start + 500). What goes wrong?
choices: start + 500 wraps to 0xF4, so it fires about 16 ms after start
start + 500 overflows to 0, so it never fires
Nothing: it fires at exactly 500 ms
It fires 500 ms late, after the next wrap
why: start + 500 = 0x000000F4 after the wrap. When millis() is 0xFFFFFF10, only 16 ms in, it is already ≥ 0xF4, so the timeout fires ~484 ms early. Only the subtraction form is always right.

q: In the superloop, a job runs when now − ping_at >= 100. Why update with ping_at += 100 rather than ping_at = now?
choices: += keeps jobs on a fixed grid so lateness does not pile up
+= is faster: a single add instead of another call to millis()
= now would overflow the 32-bit counter once 49.7 days have passed
= now makes the job run twice whenever the loop arrives late
why: If a pass runs 3 ms late, = now shifts every later run by 3 ms and the error adds up; += period keeps the 100 ms grid and absorbs the lateness.

q: ping_at = 1000 and the loop notices at now = 1003. With ping_at += 100, when is the next ping due?
why: += 100 gives 1100: back on the 100 ms grid. ping_at = now would have made it 1103, and the 3 ms would stay forever.

q: What is the weakness of lesson 06's cooperative superloop?
choices: One slow job delays every other job
It cannot run more than three jobs
It loses ticks whenever printf blocks
Jobs drift off their grid after 49.7 days
why: A job stops only when it returns, so one 50 ms job delays all the others by 50 ms; a CPU hog freezes everything. Lesson 07's preemptive kernel removes that limit.

q: Which registers form a timer's time base?
why: Time base: PSC, ARR, CNT (how fast, how far). Events: EGR, DIER, SR. Channel: CCMR1, CCER, CCR1. Control: CR1.

q: Which bits of CR1 start a timer and turn on ARR preloading?
choices: CEN starts it; ARPE turns on ARR preload
UG starts it; OC1PE turns on ARR preload
CEN starts it; UIE turns on ARR preload
UE starts it; ARPE turns on ARR preload
why: CR1.CEN runs the counter and CR1.ARPE preloads ARR. UG is in EGR, OC1PE preloads CCR1 (in CCMR1), UIE is an interrupt enable, and UE belongs to the USART.

q: What are the base addresses of TIM3 and TIM14?
why: TIM3 is at 0x40000400 and TIM14 at 0x40002000. 0xE000E010 is SysTick and 0x40004400 is USART2.

q: What is a timer's update frequency?
why: The prescaler divides by PSC + 1, then the counter runs 0 … ARR, which is ARR + 1 counts. Both registers hold N − 1.

q: At 48 MHz, which PSC and ARR give 1 MHz counting and a 20 ms period?
why: 48 MHz / 48 = 1 MHz, so PSC = 47; 20 ms = 20 000 counts, so ARR = 19 999. PSC = 479 with ARR = 1999 gives 20 ms too, but counts at 100 kHz, not 1 MHz.

q: At 48 MHz, choose PSC and ARR for a timer that counts at 1 MHz and updates every 1 ms.
why: 48 MHz / (47 + 1) = 1 MHz, and 1000 counts = 1 ms, so ARR = 999. PSC = 4799 with ARR = 9 is 1 kHz too, but counts at 10 kHz.

q: At 48 MHz, PSC = 47 and ARR = 9999. What is the update rate?
why: 48 000 000 / (48 × 10 000) = 100 Hz: 1 MHz counting, 10 ms per period.

q: At 48 MHz you want the counter to tick every 100 µs (10 kHz). Which PSC?
why: 48 MHz / 10 kHz = 4800, and PSC holds N − 1 = 4799. 479 gives 100 kHz; 47999 gives 1 kHz.

q: At the 12 MHz reset clock, which PSC makes a timer count at 1 MHz?
why: 12 MHz / (11 + 1) = 1 MHz. 47 is the 48 MHz value, and is exactly the bug if the clock is not yet switched up.

q: Someone writes PSC = 48 and ARR = 19999 at 48 MHz, intending 50 Hz. What happens?
choices: It runs at about 49 Hz, and only a cross-check notices
It runs at exactly 50 Hz; the extra 1 is absorbed
It refuses to start, because PSC must be odd
It runs at 25 Hz, because PSC doubles the period
why: 48 MHz / (49 × 20 000) ≈ 48.98 Hz, about 2 % slow. Nothing complains; only the report line's TIM3-versus-SysTick count notices.

q: What value is in TIM3's ARR for a 20 ms frame at 1 MHz, in hex?
why: 19 999 = 0x4E1F. 0x4E20 is 20 000 (forgot the −1), 0x2F is PSC = 47, and 0xBB7F is SysTick's 47 999.

q: TIM3's PSC, ARR and CCR1 are double-buffered. What does that mean for a write?
choices: Writes go to a preload copy and take effect at the next update
It is written twice, so a glitch on one of the copies is corrected
It takes effect at once, and the old value is kept aside as a backup
It is ignored until the timer has been disabled and enabled again
why: Writes land in a preload register; the counter keeps using the shadow copy until the next update. That is what lets a PWM duty change without a malformed pulse.

q: Why write EGR = UG right after setting PSC and ARR?
choices: To force an update now, so the new values take effect
To enable the update interrupt for the very first time after reset
To clear the update flag that was left over from the reset sequence
To start the counter, which setting CEN on its own cannot do
why: UG generates an update event by software, copying the preload registers into the shadows. UIE enables the interrupt, CEN starts the counter, and UG actually sets UIF rather than clearing it.

q: After EGR = UG, the code enables UIE without clearing anything. What happens?
choices: A phantom interrupt fires at once, because UG raised UIF
Nothing: UG clears UIF as part of the update
The timer stays stopped until UIF is cleared
The first real update is skipped instead
why: UG raises UIF like any update. Clear it (SR = ~TIM_SR_UIF) before enabling UIE, or the first interrupt is a phantom.

q: PSC = 47 is written but EGR = UG is skipped; ARR = 19999 took effect at once. How long is TIM3's first period at 48 MHz?
why: The prescaler is still 0 for the first period, so 20 000 counts run at 48 MHz: 20 000 / 48 MHz ≈ 0.42 ms instead of 20 ms.

q: Which line clears only UIF in TIM3_IRQHandler?
why: Timer flags clear by writing 0, and writing 1 leaves a flag alone. ~TIM_SR_UIF writes 0 to UIF and 1 to everything else. TIM_SR_UIF is the EXTI style.

q: TIM3_IRQHandler clears its flag with TIM3->SR = TIM_SR_UIF (the EXTI style). What does the board do?
choices: The handler re-enters forever: UIF stays set
Works normally: writing 1 clears a flag on every STM32 peripheral
HardFaults, because SR is a read-only register
The compiler warns that the clearing convention is the wrong one
why: Writing 1 to UIF leaves it set and writing 0 to every other bit clears them. The handler returns with UIF still pending and runs again forever. It builds with zero warnings.

q: What 32-bit value does TIM3->SR = ~TIM_SR_UIF write (UIF is bit 0)?
why: ~0x00000001 = 0xFFFFFFFE: a 0 in bit 0 clears UIF, 1s everywhere else leave the other flags alone.

q: By lesson 06, how do the three flags seen so far clear?
choices: EXTI: write 1; TIM SR: write 0; CC1IF: read CCR1
EXTI: write 0; TIM SR: write 1; CC1IF: read CCR1
All three clear by writing 1 to the flag
EXTI: read; TIM SR: write 0; CC1IF: write 1
why: Same chip, three conventions. The guide's lesson: for every flag, look up how it clears.

q: In PWM mode 1 (OC1M = 110), when is the pin high?
why: Mode 1 drives the pin high while the count is below CCR1 and low after, until ARR wraps the counter.

q: Why is CCR1 the pulse width in microseconds in this lesson?
choices: The counter ticks once per microsecond (1 MHz)
CCR1 is defined in microseconds by the hardware
The ISR converts CCR1 to microseconds each frame
ARR is 19999, which scales CCR1 to microseconds
why: With PSC = 47 at 48 MHz the counter counts at 1 MHz, so one count is one microsecond and CCR1 = 1500 means 1.5 ms.

q: How involved is the CPU in each PWM edge on PA6?
choices: Not at all; the ISR only changes CCR1
It toggles the pin in the update ISR every edge
It sets the pin at the update and clears it in a compare ISR
It polls CNT and writes BSRR at CCR1
why: The timer drives the pin by itself. The CPU is involved in no edge; the update ISR only moves CCR1.

q: Which four things turn on TIM3 channel 1 PWM output on a pin?
choices: CCMR1 mode + OC1PE, CCER.CC1E, CR1.ARPE, and the pin's AF
DIER.UIE, SR.UIF, EGR.UG, and the pin's MODER output
CCMR1 mode, CCR1, PSC, and the NVIC enable
CCER.CC1P, CCER.CC1NP, CR1.CEN, and the pin's pull-up
why: Mode and preload in CCMR1, CC1E to connect the channel to the pin, ARPE, and the alternate function on the pin. Interrupts and NVIC are not needed for the waveform.

q: What does OC1PE (CCR1 preload) guarantee when the ISR changes the pulse width?
choices: A pulse is never cut in half: changes wait for the next frame
The pulse width changes at once, even in the middle of a pulse
The new value is ignored until software writes EGR = UG again
The output is forced low for as long as CCR1 is being written
why: With preload on, every change to CCR1 takes effect at the next update, the frame boundary, so no malformed pulse is produced.

q: TIM3 counts at 1 MHz with ARR = 19999. CCR1 = 1250. What is on PA6?
why: One count is 1 µs, so CCR1 = 1250 is 1.25 ms high, and ARR + 1 = 20 000 counts is the 20 ms frame.

q: What CCMR1 value sets OC1M = 110 (bits 6:4) and OC1PE (bit 3)?
why: 0b110 << 4 = 0x60, plus 1 << 3 = 0x08, gives 0x68. 0x60 forgets the preload.

q: What does a hobby servo read, nominally?
choices: A pulse every 20 ms: 1.0 ms one end, 1.5 ms centre, 2.0 ms other end
A pulse every 1 ms: 20 % one end, 50 % centre, 80 % other end
A pulse every 20 ms: 0 ms one end, 10 ms centre, 20 ms other end
A voltage: 0 V one end, 1.65 V centre, 3.3 V other end
why: The pulse width is the whole message; the 50 Hz frame rate is not critical. Real servos differ (Arduino uses 544–2400 µs), so the lab measures it.

q: Lab check T9: PSC is changed so TIM3 counts at 2 MHz; ARR = 19999 and CCR1 = 1500 are unchanged. What happens?
choices: 100 updates/s, and the pulse shrinks to 0.75 ms
50 updates/s, and the pulse stays 1.5 ms
25 updates/s, and the pulse grows to 3 ms
100 updates/s, and the pulse stays 1.5 ms
why: At 2 MHz the frame is 20 000 × 0.5 µs = 10 ms, so 100 updates/s, and 1500 counts are only 750 µs. CCR1 still holds the pulse width, now in half-microseconds.

q: TIM3_CH1 is AF1 on PA6. What is it on PB6?
why: AF numbers depend on the pin: TIM3_CH1 is AF1 on PA6 (and PB4, PC6) but AF12 on PB6 and AF11 on PB7. The number comes from the datasheet table.

q: Which AF connects TIM14_CH1 to PA7?
why: TIM14_CH1 is AF4 on PA7 (but AF0 on PB1).

q: TIM3 is set up correctly but PA6 is given the wrong AF number. What do you see?
choices: The timer counts and interrupts at 50/s, but the servo never moves
The timer refuses to start counting until the AF number is corrected
A HardFault occurs the first time the timer tries to drive the pin
The PWM comes out on a different pin, the one that AF belongs to
why: With a wrong AF the timer works and the pin doesn't. Everything internal looks fine, including the self-test.

q: PA6 needs AF1 and PA7 needs AF4. What does GPIOA->AFR[0] hold for just those two pins?
What does the TIM3 update ISR do with SLEW?
choices: Moves CCR1 toward the target by at most SLEW µs per frame
Sets CCR1 straight to the target, then waits SLEW µs
Skips SLEW frames between servo updates
Adds SLEW µs of dead time between pulses
why: It is a rate limiter, the smallest control loop: measure, compare, correct, once per period. The servo glides instead of snapping.

q: SLEW = 20 µs per 20 ms frame. How long does the servo take to glide from 1000 µs to 2000 µs?
why: 1000 µs / 20 µs = 50 frames, and 50 × 20 ms = 1 s: 1000 µs of travel per second.

q: Lab check T4: SERVO_SLEW_US goes from 20 to 200. How many frames from 1000 µs to 2000 µs now?
why: 1000 / 200 = 5 frames, 100 ms: the servo now nearly snaps.

q: Why measure the echo with input capture instead of an EXTI interrupt reading the time?
choices: The hardware copies CNT into CCR1 at the edge; latency doesn't matter
Capture runs from a faster clock than the EXTI block, so it is finer
EXTI cannot interrupt on both edges of the same pin, only on one
Capture needs no interrupt at all, so the CPU is never even told
why: The timestamp is taken before the interrupt is even requested; latency changes when you read it, not what it says. EXTI can do both edges; the ISR still reads CCR1.

q: How is CC1IF cleared in the capture ISR?
why: Reading CCR1 clears CC1IF: the third clearing convention, and the only one needing no write.

q: TIM14 counts µs and wraps at 65536. The rising edge is captured at 65000 and the falling at 1000. What width does (uint16_t)(t_fall − t_rise) give?
why: (1000 − 65000) mod 65536 = 1536: 536 counts to the wrap plus 1000 after. The 16-bit subtraction is right across one wrap, like millis().

q: How long until a 16-bit TIM14 counting at 1 MHz wraps?
why: 2¹⁶ µs = 65.536 ms. The longest HC-SR04 echo, 400 cm, is 23.2 ms, so at most one wrap can happen between edges.

q: TIM14 capture is configured but only CC1P is set, for rising edges. What does the report show?
choices: No widths, ever: there is no falling edge to subtract
Widths twice as long as the real echo
Correct widths, since the fall is implied
A HardFault at the first echo
why: From the silent-failure list: capture both edges, or you only ever have rising timestamps and no width.

q: The guide's figure for the HC-SR04 echo is about how much per centimetre?
why: Round-trip at ~340 m/s is ~58 µs per cm. Wokwi's model is actually 58.8 µs per cm.

q: An echo is 2900 µs wide. At 58 µs per cm, how far is the object?
Lab check T3: PING_MS goes from 100 to 50. How fast does the EXTI edge count grow now?
why: 20 pings a second, two edges per echo (rise and fall): 40 edges a second, up from 20.

q: Wokwi does not implement timer input capture. How does lesson 06 still measure the echo there?
choices: EXTI line 7 interrupts on both edges and reads TIM14->CNT itself
It polls PA7 in main() and reads millis()
It uses TIM3's capture channel instead of TIM14's
It estimates the width from the servo position
why: The handler reads TIM14->CNT on each edge. Both timestamps are late by about the same latency, so the width is still right while nothing delays one of the two interrupts.

q: The capture ISR writes echo_us and echo_count together. Why does main() read them between __disable_irq() and __enable_irq()?
choices: So a capture between the two loads can't pair a new count with an old width
Because each variable on its own could tear on a 32-bit core like this one
So that the capture itself is delayed until main() has finished reading
Because volatile variables cannot be read while interrupts are enabled
why: Each word alone is safe, but the pair is one logical value. Masking for two loads keeps the pair consistent. The capture is not delayed: the hardware already took the timestamp; the interrupt just waits pending.

q: While main() reads the pair with interrupts masked, an echo edge arrives. What happens to the measurement?
choices: It is still exact: CCR1 already holds the time
It is lost: an edge that arrives while masked is never captured
It is late by the length of the masked window, a few microseconds
It is captured twice, once now and once when interrupts are re-enabled
why: Capture is hardware; the interrupt is merely held pending until __enable_irq(). The window is two loads, a fraction of a microsecond.

q: Lesson 06 gives TIM14 capture priority 1, TIM3 update 2, SysTick 3. What rule is that?
choices: Deadline-monotonic: the shorter the deadline, the more urgent
Importance to the user: the servo matters most
IRQ number order: the lowest number is most urgent
Rate order: whoever interrupts most often is most urgent
why: Capture must be read before the next edge, TIM3 has 20 ms of slack, and a late tick is still counted. Importance to the user is not the criterion.

q: A student argues: 'the servo is what the user sees, so TIM3 should be priority 0.' What is the guide's answer?
choices: Wrong: TIM3 has 20 ms of slack; priority follows deadline
Right: the output the user can see always gets the top priority
Right: PWM must be serviced by the CPU on every edge of the pulse
Wrong: TIM3 must be the least urgent, below SysTick's priority 3
why: The CPU is in no PWM edge and the update ISR has a whole 20 ms frame. The capture read has the tightest deadline.

q: TIM3 (IRQ 16) and TIM14 (IRQ 19) are both pending at the same NVIC priority. What happens?
choices: Neither preempts; TIM3 runs first, then TIM14
TIM14 preempts TIM3, as the higher IRQ number
They run interleaved, one instruction each
why: Equal priorities never preempt each other; they queue, and the lower IRQ number goes first.

q: NVIC priority bytes hold prio << 6. What byte gives TIM14 priority 1?
why: With 2 priority bits at the top of the byte, 1 << 6 = 0x40. Priority 2 is 0x80 and 3 is 0xC0.

q: Counting TIM3 updates per SysTick second should give what number?
why: Two independent clock paths from the same 48 MHz must agree: 1 s / 20 ms = 50.

q: Lab check T8: REPORT_MS goes from 1000 to 250, and 'TIM3 n/s' now reads about 12. Is TIM3 slower?
choices: No: it counts updates per report, now a quarter second
Yes: TIM3 shares its clock with the report, so it slows down too
Yes: the report now preempts TIM3 four times as often as before
No: SysTick itself slowed down by a factor of four, not TIM3
why: The number is updates − last_updates per report interval: 50 × 0.25 ≈ 12.5. The timer is unchanged; the label says /s.

q: Forgetting the RCC clock gate for TIM3 gives which symptom?
choices: The timer counts at the reset 12 MHz
The first period is at the wrong rate
why: Without the clock gate the peripheral is unpowered: writes are lost, reads return 0. The wrong-rate first period is the missing UG.

q: PWM is configured but CCER.CC1E is never set. What happens?
choices: The timer runs but the pin is dead, as with a wrong AF
The timer does not count at all
The pin outputs a constant high
why: CC1E connects the channel to the pin. Without it the counter, the interrupt and the report all look fine and the channel never reaches the pin.

q: TIM3_IRQHandler is misspelled as TIM3_IRQhandler. What happens?
choices: The vector stays Default_Handler, and the board hangs
The linker stops with an undefined-symbol error for TIM3_IRQHandler
Nothing goes wrong: the compiler matches handler names case-insensitively
Nothing goes wrong: the NVIC finds the handler by its IRQ number
why: The handler is found by its exact name: the weak alias stays in the table and the real function is never called. It builds with no error.

q: The proximity bar lights (200 − cm) × 8 / 200 LEDs as the mask (1 << lit) − 1. Which mask at 150 cm?
